identification.summary: UNC3890 is a Mandiant-tracked cluster of intrusion activity targeting Israeli organizations in shipping, government, energy, aviation and healthcare, tracked since at least late 2020 and still active in mid-2022 [S1]. Mandiant treats it as a standalone group, not classified as a TEMP, APT or FIN [S1]. It uses two custom tools, the SUGARUSH backdoor and the SUGARDUMP browser credential stealer, plus public tools [S1].
identification.firstObserved: Mandiant: tracked since at least late 2020; some credential-harvesting domains date to late 2020 [S1].
identification.notes: UNC designation is Mandiant's; no Microsoft name, MITRE group ID or other-vendor alias was found in the sources gathered. Mandiant's own text separates UNC3890 from UNC757 and UNC2448 (APT35-linked), which it cites only as comparison points [S1].

attribution.sponsor: Mandiant assesses an Iran nexus; no specific Iranian agency is named [S1].
attribution.confidence: Mandiant: moderate confidence in an Iran nexus [S1]. No government attribution was found.
attribution.basis: Mandiant cites Farsi strings in SUGARDUMP (including 'KHODA' and 'yaal', the latter also the .NET project name), Israel-focused targeting consistent with Iranian actors (UNC757), a PDB path similar to one used by UNC2448 (rated weak because the path is generic), and use of the public NorthStar C2 favored by Iranian actors (rated circumstantial) [S1].

objectives: Mandiant assesses the primary objective appears to be espionage and intelligence collection; the stolen data could support hack-and-leak operations or kinetic attacks against shipping [S1].

targeting.notes: Some targeted shipping companies are global, so impact may extend beyond Israel, but Mandiant had no confirmed targeting outside Israel [S1]. Lookalike credential-harvesting domains impersonated LinkedIn, Facebook, Office 365, Citrix and Pfizer [S1]. Some infrastructure hosted scraped Facebook and Instagram data of individuals, possibly for targeting or lures [S1].

capabilities.summary: Initial access via a watering hole on a login page of a likely compromised legitimate Israeli shipping company, which sent visitor data to a Punycode lookalike domain (lirıkedin[.]com), active at least until November 2021 [S1]. Credential-harvesting sites imitate LinkedIn, Facebook, Office 365, Citrix and Pfizer [S1]. Social-engineering lures included fake AI robotic doll commercials delivering SUGARDUMP (SMTP version) and a fake LexisNexis developer job offer in a macro-enabled .xls delivering SUGARDUMP (HTTP version) [S1]. SUGARUSH is a custom backdoor that creates a 'Service1' service and opens a reverse shell over TCP 4585 to a hardcoded C2 [S1]. SUGARDUMP harvests saved passwords from Chrome, Edge and Opera (later Firefox) and exfiltrates via email (SMTP, through Yandex, Yahoo and Gmail accounts) or HTTP; Mandiant describes three versions (early 2021 local-only, late 2021 to early 2022 SMTP, April 2022 HTTP with AES-CBC encryption) [S1]. Persistence uses scheduled tasks named to mimic Microsoft Edge/IE crash reporters [S1]. Public tools used: Metasploit, Unicorn (PowerShell downgrade and shellcode injection) and NorthStar C2 [S1]. Secondary coverage confirms the tooling and lures [S2][S3].

campaigns.name: Credential-harvesting infrastructure established
campaigns.summary: Mandiant reports lookalike domains hosting fake login pages, some dating to late 2020, marking the earliest tracked activity.

campaigns.name: Early SUGARDUMP version
campaigns.summary: First SUGARDUMP variant saved credentials locally to a text file or printed them, with no exfiltration.

campaigns.name: Israeli shipping watering hole
campaigns.summary: A login page of a likely compromised Israeli shipping company sent visitor data to a Punycode LinkedIn lookalike domain, active at least until November 2021.

campaigns.name: SUGARDUMP SMTP version with robotic-doll lure
campaigns.summary: Variant dropped as a fake video file, persisted via crash-reporter-mimicking scheduled tasks and emailed stolen browser data via Yandex, Yahoo and Gmail accounts.

campaigns.name: SUGARDUMP HTTP version with fake job offer
campaigns.summary: Macro-enabled .xls posing as a LexisNexis developer job offer delivered an HTTP-exfiltrating variant using AES-CBC.

campaigns.name: Mandiant public disclosure
campaigns.summary: Mandiant Israel Research Team published the first public report on UNC3890 on 17 August 2022, stating the cluster was still active in mid-2022.

diamond.adversary: Unattributed Iran-nexus cluster, moderate confidence per Mandiant; sponsor and operators not identified [S1].
diamond.capability: Custom SUGARUSH backdoor and SUGARDUMP stealer; Metasploit, Unicorn, NorthStar C2; watering hole, phishing lures and fake login pages [S1].
diamond.infrastructure: Interconnected C2 network hosting malware, fake login pages and phishing domains; notable hosts include 128.199.6[.]246 (malware hosting and watering hole C2), 161.35.123[.]176 (SUGARUSH C2) and 143.110.155[.]195 (NorthStar C2); SMTP exfiltration via Yandex, Yahoo and Gmail accounts [S1].
diamond.victim: Israeli shipping, government, energy, aviation and healthcare organizations; some shipping firms are global [S1].
diamond.socioPolitical: Israel-focused collection consistent with Iranian interests per Mandiant; data could support hack-and-leak or kinetic action against shipping [S1].
diamond.technology: Windows endpoints with saved browser credentials, macro-enabled Office documents, and web login pages that can be compromised as watering holes [S1].

gaps: No Microsoft name, MITRE ATT&CK group ID or other-vendor alias was found for UNC3890; the Mandiant UNC designation is the only name sourced.
No state sponsor or agency is identified; Mandiant's confidence is moderate [S1].
No reporting after the August 2022 disclosure was found, so current status, retooling and any Mandiant/Google renaming are unknown.
Mandiant's weak PDB-path link to UNC2448 (APT35-linked) and the UNC757 comparison are comparative indicators only; they do not establish overlap with those clusters [S1].
Mandiant's original page (mandiant.com) and Google Cloud blog were not directly openable in this environment except via the cloud.google.com blog fetch summary; the full IOC list was not reviewed.
Kaspersky ICS CERT H2 2022 report (an imported reference in the actor record) could not be confirmed to mention UNC3890 and is not cited.
Actual impact on victims (data stolen, any leak or kinetic use) is not reported.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Maritime and port/shipping logistics, energy and healthcare entities, plus the web login portals and webmail accounts of shipping firms, are key terrain; Mandiant notes stolen data could support kinetic attacks on shipping [S1]. STEP 2: Environment includes macro-enabled Office documents, browser-stored credentials and trusted partner login pages [S1]. STEP 3: Template is watering hole or lure (video, job offer), then SUGARDUMP credential theft with email or HTTP exfiltration, then SUGARUSH reverse shell [S1]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued credential theft and collection against Israeli and global shipping-related targets. MDCOA is use of collected data in a crisis for hack-and-leak or to support kinetic targeting of shipping, as Mandiant cautions [S1]. Candidate indicators: outbound SMTP from endpoints to Yandex, Yahoo or Gmail, scheduled tasks mimicking Edge/IE crash reporters, CrashReporter.exe or CrashLog.txt in AppData, a service named 'Service1', TCP 4585 reverse shells, and Punycode lookalike domains [S1].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track UNC3890 indicators across maritime, energy and healthcare partners, noting Mandiant confirmed targeting only in Israel [S1]. (2) Authorities: attribution is vendor-level, moderate confidence only; do not treat it as government attribution when framing response or sharing [S1]. (3) Mission assurance: shipping and logistics partners with credential reuse expose supply nodes; enforce MFA and macro restrictions and hunt for the listed host artifacts [S1]. (4) Coordination: share indicators through established partner and vendor channels and re-check for newer reporting, since none after August 2022 was found.
